newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Murdoch gains entry to U.S. satellite TV market.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Murdoch gains entry to U.S. satellite TV market.

text.p: Rupert Murdoch's News Corp. teamed up Wednesday with the nation's biggest cable television operators to form a new company that will be the No. 2 satellite television service in the United States.

PrimeStar Partners -- the satellite TV service owned by the cable companies -- said it would restructure into a public company that will include satellites and other assets from News Corp. and MCI Communications Corp.
The deal follows News Corp.'s failed efforts to join forces with EchoStar Communications Corp. Their proposed $1 billion deal collapsed into a morass of litigation.

"I couldn't quite say this is a replacement, but because that deal didn't work out, this is the next one we're doing," News Corp. spokesman Jim Platt said. "This is a way for us to recoup our investment in the satellites."
PrimeStar, with about 1.8 million subscribers, said the new assets will help it compete in the fast-growing small-dish satellite TV business.
Analysts said the deal would create a strong competitor to DirecTV, the nation's largest satellite TV service owned by Hughes Electronics Corp. and AT&T Corp.
But consumer advocates and others already were criticizing the venture, calling it another deal that violates the spirit of competition envisioned by last year's communications law.
"There's a very good chance that citizens groups will oppose the deal before the FCC and also on antitrust grounds," said Andrew Schwartzman of the Media Access Project.

Aside from the Federal Communications Commission, the Justice Department or the Federal Trade Commission will review the transaction. FCC regulators said they would examine the proposed transaction closely.

"It is a major development in the market," Peter Cowhey, head of the agency's international bureau, said in Washington. "It will get close scrutiny." He said the FCC "will want to know how this is going to affect the market for multichannel video services."

Under the new ownership structure, the current PrimeStar partners -- Time Warner Inc., Tele-Communications Inc., Cox Communications, U S West Media Group, Comcast Corp. and GE American Communications Inc. -- will contribute their interests and subscribers to the new public company, PrimeStar Inc., in return for a combination of stock and cash.
In exchange for the satellites, News Corp. and MCI will get a non-voting stake in PrimeStar Inc. worth about $1.1 billion, PrimeStar said in a statement.

PrimeStar Partners Chairman James Gray will be chairman of the new company until the restructuring is completed, when Daniel O'Brien, president of Time Warner Satellite Services Inc., will become president.
Gray said News Corp. will not get preferential treatment for its local programming on the PrimeStar system.
"News Corp. will not have a strong influence on either the management and operations or the directional strategies of PrimeStar" and their role will be "very passive," he said.
Cai von Rumohr at Cowen & Co. estimated DirecTV has about 2.6 million subscribers while No. 3 EchoStar has about 600,000. Other analysts said the two biggest players could dominate the market.

"There are very few businesses that have more than two dominant players; for Coke there is Pepsi. You are seeing the developement of a duopoly" in the direct broadcast satellite business, said PaineWebber analyst Chistopher Dixon.
EchoStar probably will seek a new partner, analysts said.
"The last piece of the puzzle will be who will be their partner," said Marc Crossman at Rauscher Pierce Refsnes.

Time Warner rose 75 cents to $50.375, Cox rose 25 cents to $25.25, U S West Media Group fell 25 cents to $21.875, News Corp. gained 25 cents to $18 and General Electric rose 37.5 cents to $62.625, all on the New York Stock Exchange.
MCI stock fell 94 cents to $40.50, Comcast fell 37.5 cents to $21.8125 and Tele-Communications was little changed at $16.94, all on Nasdaq.
